text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Private sector groups, including the Employers' Federation of New South Wales, yesterday reacted coolly to the Howard Government's work-for-the-dole plan, warning that the scheme is unlikely to make the young long-term jobless any more attractive to them as potential employees. Page 1.

Federal Sex Discrimination Commissioner Sue Walpole is to step down at the end of this month amid speculation she is concerned about proposed new legislation which she believed would downgrade her role. Walpole has cited personal reasons for her resignatin, which comes 11 months before the official end of her term. Page 1.

In a result Treasurer Peter Costello described as an indication of continued jobs growth in the economy, the new ANZ job advertisement series showed the first trend increase in the number of job ads in two years, rising 0.1 percent during January. Page 3.

The Australian Securities Commission is preparing new extradition papers against Australia's most famous corporate fugitive, Christopher Skase, in the chance that he may one day travel to a country where Australia has a better extradition agreement than the one held with Spain where Skase now calls home. Documents are being assembled to meet the "full evidence brief" to meet the strictest requirements for extradition proceedings. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Following a move by the ALP and minor parties, who combined in the Senate last night to defeat the Federal Government's special legislation to allow the controversial Hindmarsh Island bridge to go ahead, the Coalition could be forced to call another A$1 million inquiry into the bridge. Page 1.

Tributes flowed in yesterday following the death, aged 92, of Edna Ryan, the woman who stood at the forefront of the struggle for equal pay for most of this century and played "political godmother" to a generation of modern women activists. Ryan was still actively campaigning for women's equality in the workplace up to the time of her death. Page 1.

As the Federal Government attempted to defend its controversial plan to trial compulsory work for the dole for unemployed youth, Governor-General Sir William Deane called yesterday for a national effort to deal with youth unemployment, highlighting the need to restore self-esteem among the jobless. Page 1.

Professor Allan Snyder, a Harvard graduate now working at the Australian National University who has established a Centre for the Mind to study how the human mind breaks down mental barriers to achieve innovations, was awarded the Australia Prize in Canberra yesterday for his work in establishing the optical fibre network. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Following concerns expressed publicly by Environment Protection Authority chairman David Harley about polluted waters in Sydney Harbour posing a health threat to swimmers after the heavy rains a fortnight ago, Sydney Water has proposed a radical A$400 million tunnel and treatment plan to clean up the harbour, cutting the raw sewerage pollution from the two worst overflows on the north side by 80 percent. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard's office confirmed last night the government's controversial work-for-the-dole scheme will involve a move away from universal treatment of the unemployed, with local communities to decide, through submissions to the government, whether the work is voluntary or compulsory. Page 1.

In a move which has outraged pensioners who fear they will have to sell their homes, the federal government unveiled new legislation yesterday that will see nursing home operators allowed to charge the frail elderly an average entry fee of A$26,000 to gain a bed. The uncapped system of entry fees known as accommodation bonds is to be introduced from July 1. Page 1.

The world's largest floating offshore oil facility, a joint venture between Woodside, BHP and Shell, is to begin operating in 1999, 550 km north-west of Darwin. The companies will invest more than A$1 billion to extract the 250 million barrels in known reserves from the Timor Sea. The project is expected to cut Australia's current account deficit by A$1.8 billion every year for the next 14 years. Page 3.
THE AGE

The Victorian Government has ordered a review into the state's final secondary year of schooling - the Victorian Certificate of Education - to see if the year-long assessments are placing too much stress on students. A committee has been asked to look at demands placed on students for the VCE year and to find ways of reducing "unnecessary stress" without compromising the "rigor" of the final education year. Page A1.

The Federal Government's work-for-the-dole scheme faces defeat in the Senate with two key independents indicating they might back the opposition parties in voting against the bill. Employer groups also slammed the proposal, claiming it would encourage job-shedding and posed a danger for small businesses. Page A1.

Victorian child-protection workers have accused the State Government of altering documents to cover-up allegations of drug abuse and violence in state-run institutions. Although the Human Services Department was warned to stop the practice in 1995, The Age has obtained documents revealing doctored incident reports. Page A1.

Aboriginal leaders fear the Federal Government may be seeking to divide their community in the lead-up to key negotiations arising out of the High Court's Wik ruling. The fear arises from the exclusion of main Aboriginal representative bodies from legal negotiations which will pre-empt Friday's round-table negotiations. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
